subject: physics

items.q: A lamp and a resistor are connected in series with a cell. An ammeter between the cell and the lamp reads 0.30 A. A second ammeter is placed between the lamp and the resistor. What does it read?
items.correct: 0.30 A, since in series the current through each component is the same
items.misconception: Under 0.30 A, since some of the current is used up inside the lamp
items.why: Students hear that the lamp 'uses' or 'consumes' electricity and transfer that to the current itself, rather than to the energy transferred by the charge. Charge is not used up; the same charge that enters a component leaves it. What falls across the lamp is the potential difference, not the current. In series the current is the same through every component.
items.random_wrong: 0.15 A, since the current is shared between the lamp and the resistor

items.q: A 6 V battery is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor?
items.correct: 4 V
items.misconception: 3 V
items.why: 'Shared' is read as 'shared equally', as it usually is in everyday language, and the resistances are not used at all. The total potential difference of the supply is shared between the components in proportion to their resistances, because the same current is in each and V = I R. Equal shares occur only when the resistances are equal.
items.random_wrong: 6 V

items.q: A 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Which statement about the total resistance of the pair is correct?
items.correct: It is less than 3 Ω, below the smaller of the two resistances
items.misconception: It is 9 Ω, because the two resistances are added together
items.why: R_total = R_1 + R_2 is the only resistance equation given in this section, so it gets applied to every combination of resistors regardless of how they are joined. R_total = R_1 + R_2 applies only to resistors joined in series. For two resistors in parallel the total is less than the smallest of them; a numerical value is not required at GCSE.
items.random_wrong: It is 4.5 Ω, the value halfway between the two resistances

items.q: A 5 Ω resistor and a 7 Ω resistor are connected in series. What single resistance could replace them without changing the current drawn from the supply?
items.misconception: 6 Ω
items.why: Students know the answer is not the sum, and averaging feels like a safe compromise that keeps the answer 'between' the two given numbers. The total resistance of two resistors in parallel lies below both values, not between them, because the extra branch lets more current flow for the same potential difference.

items.q: Which equation gives the total resistance of two resistors joined in series?
items.correct: R_total = R_1 + R_2
items.misconception: R_total = R_1 − R_2
items.why: The rule is half-remembered as 'the total is the smallest resistor' rather than 'less than the smallest resistor', helped by the idea that charge chooses one route. Both branches carry current, because both have the full supply potential difference across them. The extra branch adds to the total current, so the total resistance is below 5 Ω, not equal to it.
items.random_wrong: R_total = R_1 × R_2

items.q: In a dc series circuit the potential difference across one resistor is 12 V and the current through it is 4 A. What is the resistance of this resistor?
items.correct: 3 Ω
items.misconception: 3 V
items.why: Units are treated as labels that travel with the numbers rather than as properties of the quantity being calculated, so the unit of the first value in the calculation is carried into the answer. Each quantity has its own unit whatever it was calculated from. Potential difference is in volts, current is in amps, and resistance, R, is in ohms, Ω.
items.random_wrong: 3 A

items.q: Two lamps are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. What is the potential difference across the lamps?
items.correct: 12 V across each lamp
items.misconception: 6 V across each lamp
items.why: The series sharing rule is applied to a parallel circuit, because 'sharing' is remembered as a general rule for circuits with more than one component. Sharing of potential difference applies to components in series. Components in parallel are connected across the same two points, so each has the full supply potential difference across it.
items.random_wrong: 24 V across each lamp

items.q: Two resistors are connected in parallel. The current in one branch is 0.4 A and the current in the other branch is 0.6 A. What is the reading on an ammeter in the main circuit, between the battery and the branches?
items.why: 'The current is the same through each component' is learned for series circuits and then remembered as a rule about all circuits. The same current through each component is a rule for series connection only. In parallel the supply current divides between the branches, and the branch currents add to give the total.

items.q: A student wants to measure both the current through a resistor and the potential difference across it. How should the two meters be connected?
items.correct: Ammeter in series with the resistor, voltmeter across it
items.misconception: Ammeter across the resistor, voltmeter in series with it
items.why: Once students learn that a voltmeter goes across a component, the two meters get swapped; 'not interfering with the circuit' is also misread as staying out of the loop. An ammeter must carry the current it measures, so it goes in series with the component. In series there is the same current through each component, so the meter reads the current in that component.
items.random_wrong: Both meters connected in series with the resistor

items.q: Explain why adding a second resistor in series with the first increases the total resistance of the circuit.
items.correct: There is one path, so charge passes through both resistors and the opposition adds
items.misconception: The first resistor uses up some of the current, leaving less to push round the loop
items.why: Students hear that the lamp 'uses' or 'consumes' electricity and transfer that to the current itself, rather than to the energy transferred by the charge. Charge is not used up; the same charge that enters a component leaves it. What falls across the lamp is the potential difference, not the current. In series the current is the same through every component.
items.random_wrong: The extra resistor creates a second path, so the charge is held back more strongly

items.q: Explain why adding a second resistor in parallel with the first decreases the total resistance of the circuit.
items.correct: The extra branch is another path for charge, so more current is drawn from the supply
items.misconception: The two resistors share the current, so each of them has less work to do than before
items.why: 'The current splits' is remembered as 'the current halves', and the role of resistance in deciding each branch current is overlooked. Each branch has the same potential difference across it, so the branch with the lower resistance carries the larger current. The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components.
items.random_wrong: Adding a resistor must add resistance, so the total is larger than either of them

items.q: A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor. What is the current in the circuit?
items.why: The supply potential difference is used with a single component's resistance, because students apply V = I R to one resistor at a time without first finding the total resistance or the shared potential differences. Use the supply potential difference only with the total resistance R_total = R_1 + R_2. That gives the one current in the series loop; each resistor's own potential difference then follows from V = I R for that resistor.

items.q: A 6 Ω resistor and a 9 Ω resistor are connected in series with a 30 V supply. Using the equivalent resistance of the pair, what is the current in the circuit?
items.why: The supply potential difference is used with a single component's resistance, because students apply V = I R to one resistor at a time without first finding the total resistance or the shared potential differences. Use the supply potential difference only with the total resistance R_total = R_1 + R_2. That gives the one current in the series loop; each resistor's own potential difference then follows from V = I R for that resistor.

items.q: A resistor is tested using a dc circuit in which the resistor, an ammeter and a variable resistor are joined in series, with a voltmeter across the resistor. Why is this a good design for the test?
items.correct: The ammeter reads the current in the resistor itself, and the variable resistor changes it
items.misconception: The variable resistor alters the potential difference of the supply, so several values can be tested
items.why: A variable resistor is treated like a volume control, where 'more' always means a bigger effect, and the inverse relationship between resistance and current is not applied. For a fixed supply potential difference, a larger total resistance gives a smaller current. Since the components are in series, that smaller current is the current through every component.
items.random_wrong: The ammeter is kept in parallel, so it does not change the current in the resistor under test

items.q: In the series test circuit above, the resistance of the variable resistor is increased. What happens to the current through the component under test?
items.correct: It falls, because the total resistance of the series circuit is now larger
items.misconception: It rises, because a larger resistance gives the charges a bigger push round
items.why: A variable resistor is treated like a volume control, where 'more' always means a bigger effect, and the inverse relationship between resistance and current is not applied. For a fixed supply potential difference, a larger total resistance gives a smaller current. Since the components are in series, that smaller current is the current through every component.
items.random_wrong: It is unchanged, because the current in a series circuit is always the same

items.q: Two lamps are lit by one battery. One lamp is unscrewed from its holder and the other stays lit at the same brightness. What does this show?
items.correct: They are in parallel: the remaining lamp still has a complete path and the same potential difference
items.misconception: They are in series: the current simply carries on round the rest of the single loop
items.why: Charge is imagined as flowing out of the cell to each component in turn, rather than round one continuous path that has to be complete. In series there is a single path, so there must be an unbroken route through every component. A break anywhere stops the current everywhere in that loop.
items.random_wrong: They are in parallel, so the remaining lamp now takes the share of the one removed

items.q: A circuit diagram shows a cell, a switch and two identical lamps drawn one after another in a single loop. Which statement is correct when the switch is closed?
items.correct: Both lamps light, with the same current through each of them
items.misconception: Both light, but the lamp nearer the positive terminal is brighter
items.why: Charge is pictured as travelling round the loop 'spending' energy as it goes, so whatever it reaches first is imagined to receive the most. The order of components in a series loop does not change how the potential difference is shared. The share depends on the resistances, and the current is the same at every point in the loop.
items.random_wrong: Both light, with the full potential difference of the cell across each

items.q: A 9 V supply is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 7 Ω resistor. Which statement about the potential differences is correct?
items.correct: 2 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 7 V across the 7 Ω resistor
items.misconception: 4.5 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 4.5 V across the 7 Ω resistor
items.why: 'Shared' is read as 'shared equally', as it usually is in everyday language, and the resistances are not used at all. The total potential difference of the supply is shared between the components in proportion to their resistances, because the same current is in each and V = I R. Equal shares occur only when the resistances are equal.
items.random_wrong: 9 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 9 V across the 7 Ω resistor

items.q: A 4 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Which of these values could be the total resistance of the pair?
items.correct: 3 Ω
items.why: R_total = R_1 + R_2 is the only resistance equation given in this section, so it gets applied to every combination of resistors regardless of how they are joined. R_total = R_1 + R_2 applies only to resistors joined in series. For two resistors in parallel the total is less than the smallest of them; a numerical value is not required at GCSE.
items.random_wrong: 8 Ω

items.q: A resistor is connected in series with a battery, and this resistor supplies two further resistors that are connected in parallel with each other. Which statement about this circuit is correct?
items.correct: The current in the series resistor equals the sum of the two branch currents
items.misconception: The current in the series resistor equals the current in each of the branches
items.why: 'The current is the same through each component' is learned for series circuits and then remembered as a rule about all circuits. The same current through each component is a rule for series connection only. In parallel the supply current divides between the branches, and the branch currents add to give the total.
items.random_wrong: The potential difference of the battery is shared equally by all three resistors

items.q: Two identical lamps are in series with a cell. The cell supplies a current of 0.4 A. What is the current through each lamp?
items.correct: 0.4 A through each lamp, because in series there is the same current through each component.
items.misconception: The current is shared between the components, so each lamp gets half of it, 0.2 A.
items.why: The sharing rule for series circuits is remembered but attached to the wrong quantity: it is the potential difference that is shared, not the current. In series it is the total potential difference of the power supply that is shared between the components. The current is the same through each of them.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A second resistor is connected in parallel with the first. What happens to the total resistance of the circuit?
items.correct: The total resistance falls, and becomes less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.
items.misconception: Adding another resistor must add resistance, so the total resistance goes up whichever way the resistor is connected.
items.why: The word 'resistor' is treated as something that always obstructs, so any extra one is assumed to obstruct more, without thinking about the extra path it creates. A resistor added in parallel creates an extra path for charge, so more current is drawn from the supply for the same potential difference. That means the total resistance has fallen. Only resistors added in series increase the total resistance.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where should a voltmeter be placed to measure the potential difference across a resistor?
items.correct: In parallel, connected across the resistor.
items.misconception: The voltmeter goes in the circuit loop, in series with the resistor, so that the charge passes through it.
items.why: Ammeters are met first and go in the loop, so a voltmeter is assumed to be fitted the same way; students also picture a meter as something the current must pass through to register. Potential difference is measured between two points, so the voltmeter is connected across the component, in parallel with it. Placing it in series would break the measurement and reduce the circuit current.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two resistors are in series with a 6 V battery. What is the potential difference across each resistor?
items.correct: The two potential differences are smaller than 6 V and add up to 6 V.
items.misconception: Each component in the circuit has the full 6 V of the battery across it.
items.why: The parallel rule that each component has the supply potential difference across it is applied to a series circuit, or the battery is imagined to deliver its full voltage to everything it is connected to. Each component has the full supply potential difference across it only when the components are in parallel. In series the supply potential difference is shared between the components.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two identical 10 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
items.correct: Less than 10 Ω, because the total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the smallest individual resistor.
items.misconception: The resistors are identical, so nothing changes and the total resistance is still 10 Ω.
items.why: The 'less than the smallest' rule is thought to apply only when the two resistances differ, so identical resistors are assumed to be a special case where the value stays put. The rule holds for any two resistors in parallel, identical or not. Two identical branches draw twice the current a single one would, so the total resistance is below 10 Ω.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A third identical lamp is added in series to a circuit with two lamps. What happens to the brightness of the original lamps?
items.correct: They become dimmer, because the total resistance has increased so the current in the loop is smaller.
items.misconception: Adding another lamp adds more to the circuit, so all the lamps get brighter.
items.why: 'More components' is read as 'more of everything', and the effect of the extra resistance on the current in the single series path is not considered. Resistors and lamps added in series increase the total resistance, so the current falls, and the supply potential difference is now shared between three components instead of two. All the lamps are dimmer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two lamps are connected in parallel and one of them is removed from its holder. What happens to the other lamp?
items.correct: It stays lit at the same brightness, because its own branch is still a complete path with the full supply potential difference across it.
items.misconception: The circuit is now broken, so the second lamp goes out as well.
items.why: The series experience of one broken lamp stopping everything is carried over, because a circuit is pictured as a single loop that must be complete all the way round. A parallel circuit provides more than one path. Breaking one branch leaves the other branch complete, and the potential difference across it is unchanged, so it keeps working.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.2.2 Series and parallel circuits
